Crews pumped water off Tradition Parkway and put up barricades along Port St. Lucie Boulevard on Thursday as another round of rain flooded roads in a city still recovering from storms earlier this month. Lucie police reported high water at six locations. On northbound Village Parkway near Discovery Way, water made the right lane impassable and was spreading into the next lane. Police said more closures were possible as the rain continued. Where police reported flooding Port St. Lucie Boulevard: Crews were putting up barricades at McCorkle Avenue, at Alcantara Boulevard and along the stretch from Southwest Liberty Drive to Firestone. Northbound Village Parkway: The right lane was impassable south of the fire station and south of Discovery Way. Water was spreading into a second lane near Discovery Way. Tradition Parkway east of Hazel Drive: Crews were pumping water off the road after the outside lanes flooded in both directions. Police urged drivers to take another route if they encounter standing water and to stay clear of barricades. Conditions can change quickly. Where to fill sandbags St. Lucie County says sand is still available while supplies last at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds’ west parking lot, 15601 W. Midway Road in Fort Pierce. The Lawnwood Stadium site has run out. The fairgrounds site is self-service. Bring a shovel and plan to fill your own bags. The county has a limited supply of bags and encourages residents to bring their own. Residents in unincorporated St. Lucie County can report flooding that threatens homes, businesses or personal safety to flooding@stlucieco.gov. See also: Who’s responsible for improving drainage after St. Lucie County’s historic flooding? Lucie Public Schools reopened on a regular schedule Thursday after closing Wednesday over flooding concerns. Aftercare, sports and other activities were scheduled to resume. The district said weather-related absences would be excused with a note from a parent or guardian. In neighboring Indian River County, public schools and district offices were closed Thursday. More rain on already-soaked ground A flood watch covers St. Lucie County through 7 p.m. The National Weather Service issued a separate advisory Thursday morning for northeastern St. Lucie County and eastern Indian River County after radar and gauges indicated 2 to 4 inches had already fallen across that area. 1 3 storm, one location in Port St. Lucie recorded 16.7 inches of rain over 60 hours. Lucie County had received at least 472 preliminary reports of property damage from that storm. The county is accepting damage reports from the earlier storm through Nov.

Posted Share Copy link Facebook Nextdoor X Threads Reddit LinkedIn Email WhatsApp Messenger Print Add WPTV as a Google Preferred Source WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — A movie theater is coming back to CityPlace in downtown West Palm Beach, according to Related Ross. The developer confirmed it has submitted redesign plans for the previously approved 515 Fern building to include a 35,000-square-foot movie theater with 800 seats. The building, originally approved in 2023, has also been reduced in height by 36 feet to 24 stories. “Residents have told us they miss going to the movies at CityPlace and want a movie theater back in the downtown. These changes will create a reimagined movie-going experience in the heart of West Palm Beach.” The announcement comes three years after the former movie theater at The Square closed and was demolished in 2023 to make way for new development. An opening date for the new theater has not been announced.

Lucie County Schools Superintendent Dr. Jon Prince apologized to the district Tuesday night and promised a review of all decisions and actions from the historic flooding on Nov. "It was very stressful for our families, and I certainly apologize for the stress that they went through on that day," Prince said. A video from that day shows a boy getting off a school bus on SW Coleman Avenue in Port St. Lucie and walking through flood waters that reach as high as his chest. Critics have pointed to that video and questioned the actions of the school district. In an exclusive interview, Prince expressed regret over the events of Nov. 2, stating that decisions were made based on the information available at the time. He emphasized that the flooding was unexpected. "The bottom line is I don't know of anything that could have predicted what transpired as the day progressed," Prince said. Prince assured that every decision made that day is being analyzed. "We are going to review all our procedures, our policies to make sure that if there's anything that we could have done differently, that moving forward we will," he said. With heavy rain in the forecast, St. Lucie County Schools decided to cancel classes for Wednesday. Prince said he hopes the decision is an overreaction. At the same time, though, he does not want to take any chances. "The ground is so saturated, but if the conditions worsen tomorrow, we don't want a repeat of what happened November 2," Prince said. Prince said the district will monitor the weather Wednesday and decide late Wednesday afternoon if classes should be canceled again Thursday. He said they'll follow that model until they are sure it's safe for students to return to class. Due to anticipated rainfall, at least one public-school district and a private school on the Treasure Coast will close. LUCIE COUNTY A spokesperson for the St. Lucie County Public Schools announced that the school district will be closed to students and employees on Wednesday, Nov. "While there remains some uncertainty regarding the exact timing, location, and amount of rainfall, current forecasts from the National Weather Service indicate the potential for significant rainfall and localized flooding. Given the already saturated conditions in our community, the District believes taking a cautious approach is in the best interest of our students, families, and employees," the school district spokesperson said in a statement. All after-school activities, after-care programs and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday were canceled. The spokesperson added that school district officials will continue to monitor rainfall, flooding, road closures and the accessibility of schools, bus stops and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision about school reopening on Thursday will be announced on Wednesday evening. The school district said it will provide updates on its website and social media platforms. John Carroll High School: The private school in Fort Pierce announced it will be closed on Wednesday because of the potential for heavy rainfall and flooding throughout the region. "The decision follows today's early dismissal and a review of current weather forecasts and local flooding conditions. School officials determined that closing campus is the best course of action to ensure the safety of students, faculty, staff, and families," the school said in a statement to WPBF 25 News on Tuesday evening. "All school-sponsored activities scheduled for Wednesday, including athletics, practices, extracurricular programs, and other events, have been canceled." The school added it anticipates resuming normal operations on Thursday, Nov. 19, pending weather and road conditions. "Administrators will continue to monitor forecasts and remain in communication with local authorities before making any further decisions regarding school operations," the school said. "Updates will be shared through the school’s official communication channels as conditions warrant." Boys Girls Club of Palm Beach County: All Boys Girls Club school sites in Palm Beach County are closed November 18 due to weather concerns, while other club sites remain open. Lucie County: All after-school programs and Clubhouse locations will be closed on Wednesday, Nov. MARTIN COUNTY The Martin County School District said that school and Extended Day will be open to students on Wednesday, but all other after-school activities, athletic practices and events are canceled for Wednesday. Officials in Martin County will monitor weather conditions. Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County: All Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County locations will reopen on Wednesday, Nov. 18, and resume normal operating hours. INDIAN RIVER COUNTY The School District of Indian River County announced on Tuesday afternoon that there will be a regular school schedule for students and employees, including Extended Day and extracurricular activities, on Wednesday, Nov. The wanted level in Port St. Lucie should stay at zero, police say. As Grand Theft Auto VI arrives Thursday, the Port St. Lucie Police Department posted a playful safety briefing reminding fans that real life doesn’t come with a respawn button and that U.S. 1 and Crosstown are not racetracks. Five stars might be impressive in GTA , but trust us, you don’t want that kind of attention in Port St. Lucie, the department wrote. Its other reminders: patrol vehicles aren’t available for test drives, red lights aren’t suggestions, sidewalks aren’t shortcuts and the SWAT team isn’t a feature anyone wants to unlock. What happens in Vice City stays in Vice City, the post said. Lucie might come with a police report. The game officially launches Nov. 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. Rockstar’s fictional state of Leonida draws on Florida , with Vice City serving as its Miami-inspired centerpiece. The game follows Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, whose criminal plans pull them into a conspiracy spanning the state. CBS12 has been following the Sunshine State’s transformation into a real-life part of the game’s promotion. In September, a giant pink Welcome to Vice City sign went up on Miami’s Kaseya Center as part of a deal between Miami-Dade County and Rockstar Games. County officials said the arrangement was expected to bring in nearly $1 million in revenue and create marketing opportunities. Miami has also leaned into the Vice City connection with release-week events. The Miami Heat held a Night in Vice City celebration Wednesday, the night before launch. A release-day party is planned Thursday at the Clevelander South Beach, and Rockstar’s GTA VI : The Festival is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. See also: Who’s responsible for improving drainage after St. Lucie County’s historic flooding? Police in other cities have also used the GTA VI release to remind players to keep the game’s crime on screen. The Atlanta Police Department posted that GTA is not a real place, but Atlanta is! and warned that reckless driving, drunk driving, auto theft and violence have real consequences. Keep it in the game, the department wrote . In South Florida, law enforcement leaders raised a different concern before release day. The Miami-Dade Association of Chiefs of Police opposed plans to promote the county as Vice City, saying the game depicts violence against women and law enforcement. Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz also questioned whether public agencies should promote a game built around crimes her department works to prevent. For drivers tempted to bring a little of the game’s chaos onto local roads, PSLPD’s advice is simpler: drive safe, play smart and leave the wanted level in the game. Could 'sick days' coincide with release? The release could affect more than gamers’ free time. A GameSquare survey of 1,000 U.S. employees found that 10% of full-time employees surveyed who identify as gamers planned to skip work on launch day, while another 30% were considering taking time off. Of those considering time off, 36% said they would call in sick. The survey also found that 42% expected the game to make them less productive at work. Surveyed gamers expected to spend about $400 on the game and related purchases, and anticipated playing a median of 15 hours during the opening weekend. The survey found 70% might skip watching sports to spend more time gaming, while 42% said they’d be less likely to watch NFL games that weekend. I ndian River County students have Thursday off , giving young GTA VI fans an unexpected chance to spend part of release day in Vice City. The district closed schools because of forecast conditions and flooding concerns, while St. Lucie schools reopened and Palm Beach County schools remained open, except for West Boca High School, which is closed because of heavy flooding in the parking lot.

It's the most anticipated video game in the last 10 years. At midnight Thursday, video gamers in Florida will finally have an opportunity to play Grand Theft Auto 6.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "Everything I'm seeing so far looks like the hype has been worth it," said Adriano, who was outside Skinny Louie restaurant in West Palm Beach on Wednesday. The restaurant has been rebranded as Burger Shot, a fictional fast-food place featured in the game.GTA 6, as it is being called, is set in a place that looks very much like South Florida.The game reportedly had a $1 billion budget and has generated so much buzz among fans that the Wall Street Journal estimates 1.5 million may skip work on Thursday.Sportsinsider.com reports Florida ranks first in the nation for people expected to use a PTO or vacation day to play the game."No work tomorrow or for the next five days," said Laury, who was grabbing lunch Thursday at the West Palm Burger Shot. "It's a little bit of a religious experience. It's a little crazy."GTA 6 sells for $79.99 for the standard edition and $99.99 for the ultimate edition for PlayStation 5 and Xbox.WATCH BELOW: Could GTA 6 become best-selling game of all time?"It's really reached this level of like mainstream awareness that's pretty unprecedented for a game like this," Jordan Minor, principal writer at PCMag, said. Minor wrote a review of the game, calling it "a masterpiece I never want to leave.""For a lot of other people, this is going to be the only game they play all year or all next year," Minor said. "It may be the only game they've played in like the past five years."

A Palm Beach County business owner says the deadly Learjet crash along Military Trail left her shop inaccessible for 11 days, costing her thousands of dollars.But when Denise Casselman applied for a county grant designed to help businesses impacted by the crash, she was denied.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Casselman, who owns the Auto Care Center with her husband, contacted WPTV after she said she struggled to get answers about why her business was left outside the county's grant boundaries."It means a lot," Casselman said of the business. Sandbags are available at Okeechobee County Public Works, 804 Northwest Second St. Lucie County Public Safety Department is monitoring the forecast and reminding residents to secure loose items that could be damaged by wind. Gusty northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast Tuesday and Wednesday, with gusts of 35 to 40 mph along the coast. Residents should secure tarps, patio furniture and other unsecured items. A rip current advisory remains in effect for St. Strong onshore winds can create dangerous rip currents and rough surf. Lucie County Fire District says its firefighters, paramedics and telecommunicators are prepared to respond as the area faces more heavy rain and recovers from recent flooding. Free sand is available while supplies last at two self-service locations: County Fairgrounds: 5601 W. Midway Road, Fort Pierce, in the west parking lot Lawnwood Stadium: 2000 Virginia Ave., Fort Pierce Residents should bring their own bags, shovel and other supplies. Residents can use Community Connect to share household information that could help firefighters prepare for an emergency. The county has extended the deadline to Nov. 30 for residents to report flood damage through an online survey. The survey is open to property owners and tenants throughout St. Lucie County, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated areas. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Residents can complete the flood damage survey by Nov. Officials urge residents across the region to avoid flooded roads and keep roadways clear for emergency responders. If you encounter flooding, turn around and find a safe alternate route.

Congress Ave., Boynton Beach, near the former Youfit Gym entrance next to Christ Fellowship.HOW TO HELPProperty owners, businesses and community partners with a large, accessible parking lot or open space available on Saturday mornings are encouraged to contact Restoration Bridge International.Contact: Jason Mandle, executive directorEmail: jason@restorationbridge.netWebsite For additional information, contact RBI's office at (561) 316-0399.

After five Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office deputy-involved shootings since August, WPTV is taking a closer look at how the agency trains deputies for critical encounters where decisions can be made in a matter of seconds.The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office invited WPTV's Michael Hoffman inside its immersive training simulator, which puts deputies through scenarios ranging from active shooters and potentially deadly encounters to situations where no lethal force is necessary.Hoffman participated in the training firsthand, experiencing how quickly a situation can develop and how deputies are expected to decide whether to escalate, de-escalate or rely on communication alone.The training comes at a time following five deputy-involved shootings involving the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office in recent months.Those incidents happened in:West Palm Beach on Aug. 6South Palm Beach on Sept. 10Each incident carries its own circumstances, but collectively they raise questions about how deputies prepare for encounters in which rapidly changing conditions can force them to make consequential decisions.To better understand that training, Hoffman went through it.Inside the simulator, deputies face a wide range of scenarios."We go from active shooter, and we have ones that are just completely, there's going to be no lethal force," Cpl. Capobianco, a PBSO training deputy, said.The training isn't necessarily limited to a predetermined outcome.According to Capobianco, trainers can change how a scenario develops depending on how the deputy interacts with the person on screen."We're able to choose different, how should I say, different like categories to select from to escalate, de-escalate the situation, all based off of how the deputy's communicating to the screen and how the scenario is reacting from there," Capobianco said.That means a deputy's words and actions can influence what happens next.Before Hoffman entered the simulator, trainers sat him down in a classroom and explained what he could expect.Deputies then walked him through the equipment available during training."We have every weapon platform that we have here," Capobianco said.The options include handguns, shotguns and rifles, along with Tasers and other less-lethal devices.Then, it was Hoffman's turn.He went through multiple simulated encounters designed to test how he would respond under pressure.But the scenario that stood out most did not require him to use a weapon at all.The scenario involved a man standing on a highway overpass and threatening to throw a baby.Hoffman's primary tools were his voice and his ability to de-escalate the situation."Has this gone too far already, or is there a way out?" the simulated man asked."You're not too late," Hoffman responded. "Let's just take a breath and slow this down a little bit, OK?"After the scenario ended, trainers immediately began breaking down what happened and why."You controlled the situation, right? You verbally made sure that he was making contact with you," one trainer told Hoffman.The trainer pointed specifically to Hoffman's decision not to immediately introduce a weapon into the encounter."You took the time to de-escalate the situation without having to escalate things even further by the mere presence of drawing your weapon," the trainer said.That debrief is part of the training.Rather than simply running deputies through a scenario, trainers can walk through the decisions made during an encounter and examine how communication or tactical choices affected its direction.For Hoffman, the experience showed how quickly emotion can become part of a critical encounter."I'm sure that everyone's been in a situation where they're really emotional and they're not seeing rational thought, and they have the thought to do something crazy," Hoffman said after the exercise. "But it just takes someone to take an extra second, be like, 'Hey, life is still going on. Just slow down, man.'"The scenario was simulated. The adrenaline and stress were not.And following five deputy-involved shootings in recent months, the exercise offered a firsthand look at one way PBSO trains deputies for situations in which they may have only seconds to determine what happens next.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Weisbecker said.Weisbecker was approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program, which provides housing assistance to eligible residents.While the grant offers some relief, the cost of rebuilding a flood-damaged home can quickly exceed that amount.And not every family will qualify for the same assistance."This is very urgent for people to get back into their daily lives," Weisbecker said. "This is total devastation. For everyone."New estimates released by Martin County reveal the staggering financial toll of the flooding.According to county officials, the storm caused:$14 million in beach damageNearly $1 million in damaged roads that now need to be repaved$3 million in residential losses affecting families still struggling to recoverAdditional costs in county staff overtime associated with the emergency responseThose figures put the known damage at approximately $18 million, not including additional expenses.A federal major disaster declaration could open the door to FEMA assistance for the public infrastructure repairs and potentially provide additional relief to affected residents.But so far, no such declaration has been approved.Without federal reimbursement, County Spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess said Martin County could be left responsible for covering millions of dollars in public recovery costs itself, forcing officials to find funding elsewhere in the county budget or identify other sources of assistance.And that uncertainty comes as residents are already struggling to afford repairs to their own homes.During an emotional Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, flood victims pleaded with local leaders to do more to secure financial assistance."Please. Fight for us!" one resident urged commissioners.Others questioned why help was taking so long, particularly as more rain threatened their already damaged properties."And the answer from this dais is wait 13 more days?!?" another resident asked.Commissioner Eileen Vargas of District 1 told residents she is doing everything she can to try to expedite the process, but 'doesn't have all the answers.'"I did, through contacts, reach out to FEMA to try and get this going," Vargas said.According to Vargas, a new FEMA director is expected to take office Nov. 30, which she hopes will turn the tide. "He is going to personally petition President Trump to declare our area a disaster," Vargas said.However, a federal declaration is not guaranteed, and even if approved, not all damages or recovery expenses would necessarily qualify for reimbursement.WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey contacted FEMA, questioning the length of the response and when residents could expect answers.In its response, FEMA confirmed it had received the major disaster declaration request and that the request remains under review.The agency referred additional questions about the response and recovery timeline to the Florida Division of Emergency Management.WPTV also contacted the state agency but had not received a response as of Wednesday.In the meantime, Martin County is working to distribute emergency housing assistance through Florida's SHIP program.The county currently has approximately $1 million in SHIP funding available, with eligible residents able to apply for grants of up to $25,000.Additional assistance may be available through loans of up to $75,000, though those loans are subject to repayment requirements and liens.County officials acknowledged that the existing funding could run out quickly, particularly given the scale of the destruction.Michelle Miller, Martin County's human services director, told commissioners the state has promised additional disaster relief funding, but doesn't know when that funding could come in. "They haven't confirmed the amount yet but has assured us we will be getting some disaster relief funds," Miller said.But there are limitations.Some programs require homeowners to pay for repairs upfront before seeking reimbursement. Others have income eligibility requirements that could leave struggling families without assistance."There's going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where somebody barely missed the limit," Commissioner Blake Capps said.To address that gap, Capps proposed creating a separate county-funded emergency relief program for residents who do not qualify for existing state assistance.When Hussey asked Capps whether he had identified a potential funding source for that assistance, he said where that money would come from remains unclear."Well, that would be ... we'd have to talk to staff," Capps replied. Commissioners are expected to revisit the proposal at a future meeting.For families along Hyline Drive, the uncertainty is compounded by the threat of additional rainfall.Homes have been stripped down to their frames. Belongings have been thrown away. Neighbors who spent days wading through floodwaters are now facing what could be months of repairs.Meanwhile, Martin County faces its own financial questions, with millions of dollars in public infrastructure damage and no guarantee that federal funding will cover the costs.For Weisbecker and her neighbors, every day without answers is another day they cannot fully move forward.Demolition may be the first step toward recovery.But for families who have lost nearly everything, rebuilding remains an uncertain — and potentially unaffordable — next step.

A 24-year-old woman has died from injuries she suffered after she was struck while riding an electric scooter in a hit-and-run crash in Port St. Lucie, police said Wednesday.The woman died at approximately 9:23 p.m. Tuesday, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The crash happened around 5:10 a.m. Monday near the intersection of Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace.Police said the woman was riding an electric scooter when a vehicle struck her. Investigators allege the driver left the scene without stopping to help her or notify law enforcement.The department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit later identified the vehicle as a gray Chevrolet Tahoe and located it at a Port St. Lucie home, according to police.Investigators identified the alleged driver as 18-year-old Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer.Police said investigators learned Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing "ding dong ditch" with friends shortly before the crash. According to the department, the group was leaving a home where they had been participating in the prank when the vehicle struck the woman.Sanchez-Chasmer was arrested and charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, a second-degree felony, police said.Following the woman's death, police said they anticipate the State Attorney's Office will pursue enhanced or additional charges as appropriate based on the circumstances and the outcome of the investigation.Police did not identify the woman in Wednesday's news release.

Heavy rain remains the main concern Another round of heavy rain is possible across the Treasure Coast, Okeechobee County and Palm Beach County over the next few days. Showers and isolated storms will be most common through Friday, but rainfall will vary from place to place. The main concern is that some locations could see repeated downpours and much higher totals than nearby areas, increasing the risk of street and poor-drainage flooding. Why the rain could keep returning Several parts of the atmosphere are working together to keep the rain going. High pressure to the north is pushing a steady east wind toward Florida, while a weak low-pressure system is lingering over the Gulf. A disturbance higher up in the atmosphere is helping that low hang around. Together, they are keeping a boundary across the peninsula and drawing unusually moist air into the region. As the east wind pushes showers toward the coast, the air can pile up there and help showers repeatedly form or move over the same areas. Higher totals will be localized Rainfall forecasts differ across the region, and the exact locations of the heaviest downpours remain uncertain. Across east-central Florida, including the Treasure Coast and Okeechobee County, several inches of rain are forecast through Friday, with localized totals of 8 12 inches possible, especially closer to the coast. For Palm Beach County, the current forecast calls for 2 4 inches through Thursday, with isolated higher totals of 6 8 inches and locally more than 10 inches possible. Those higher amounts would depend on repeated rounds of rain falling over the same spots. That’s why the biggest concern is for pockets of higher rainfall, rather than the same amount of rain falling evenly across all three counties. Even where totals are lower, heavy bursts could quickly flood roads and areas with poor drainage, especially where water has not had time to recede. Flood Watches remain in effect Flood Watches are in effect through Thursday evening for Palm Beach County and through Friday evening for Okeechobee County and the Treasure Coast. Hazardous conditions on the water Strong east winds will also make for hazardous conditions on the water. Atlantic seas are expected to build to 8 12 feet near South Florida, with even higher seas forecast farther north, and dangerous surf and rip currents are expected along the coast. Small craft should avoid heading out in these conditions. Drier weather expected this weekend Rain chances should ease this weekend as the low shifts north and drier air moves in. A few showers may linger Saturday, with generally drier weather expected Sunday into early next week. Moisture could begin returning around the middle of next week, though the timing and potential for more significant rain remain uncertain.

Pinewood Elementary School science teacher Richard Acosta has been named the 2026-27 Martin County Teacher of the Year, earning the opportunity to represent the county in the Florida Department of Education’s statewide Teacher of the Year competition.The Education Foundation of Martin County announced Acosta as the overall winner during its Teacher of the Year Award Celebration on Nov. 6 at the MIDFLORIDA Event Center in Port St. Lucie.Acosta was also named Elementary Teacher of the Year.“This is phenomenal,” Acosta said after the honor was revealed. “I feel incredibly invigorated and inspired to go to the next level and represent Martin County at the state competition.”Acosta was among three educators recognized with top honors.Miriam Hernández, an intensive reading teacher at Indiantown Middle School, was named Middle School Teacher of the Year.Marc Turull, who teaches International Baccalaureate physics and chemistry at South Fork High School, was named High School Teacher of the Year.Turull said the award also represents the people he works alongside.“It’s such an honor,” Turull said. “I teach physics, and I work with amazing people, so to represent them and be Teacher of the Year makes me so grateful.”Hernández described the recognition as both a privilege and an honor.During the celebration, the three teachers emphasized the importance of educators at every stage of a student's education.“The fact is that it takes all three of us for excellence in Martin County schools,” Acosta said. “We start with the foundation in elementary school. We move on to middle school intensive reading, and then we finish at the high school at South Fork. So we, we feel very blessed to be working together.”The Education Foundation said Acosta’s 35-year career in education can be traced partly to his own experience as a teenager.According to the Education Foundation of Martin County, at 16, Acosta was struggling with confidence and direction when he entered teacher John Lynskey’s American history class. According to the foundation, Lynskey’s storytelling and encouragement helped Acosta develop a love of learning.Acosta still keeps two history books Lynskey gave him.His path toward teaching became clearer when Acosta later tutored a younger student after school and watched the child's confidence and enthusiasm for learning grow, according to the foundation.Today, Acosta teaches science to students from prekindergarten through fifth grade at Pinewood Elementary.“I love what I do, and I love energizing the classroom and engaging them to the greatest possibility,” Acosta said.His lessons include hands-on investigations tied to the natural environment around Martin County. The Education Foundation said students have examined sea turtle skull models, shells and other materials connected to the Indian River Lagoon while studying how adaptations help turtles survive.Acosta also helped develop a “Birds of the Everglades” curriculum with environmental partners and has been involved with schoolwide science initiatives and family STEAM events.For Acosta, the recognition provides another opportunity beyond representing Martin County at the state level.“I feel very blessed to be in this position because I get to mentor other teachers from other schools,” Acosta said.Acosta also receives a one-year vehicle lease provided through Audi Stuart and Infiniti Stuart.“That is amazing and spectacular,” Acosta said. “I cannot wait to pick out a car on Saturday.”The celebration recognized 24 school-level Teachers of the Year who were selected by their peers. According to the Education Foundation, nominees submitted application portfolios and participated in interviews before a panel of judges.Felix A. Williams Elementary School also won the Spirit Award for its enthusiasm, interpretation of the event's theme, and props.The recognition comes as Martin County educators continue the everyday work behind the awards: helping children learn, building their confidence and creating connections that can influence students long after they leave the classroom.For Acosta, that circle is especially meaningful. A teacher once helped him see greater possibilities for his own future. Decades later, he is working to create those possibilities for another generation.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. All School District of Indian River County public schools and district offices will be closed Thursday, Nov. 19, because of expected heavy rain and potential flooding, district officials announced Wednesday. Officials cited already saturated ground and concerns about whether students and employees could safely travel to and from schools. The storm system is expected to affect Indian River, Brevard and Volusia counties between 3 a.m. Thursday, according to the district. Indian River County remains under a flood watch as another round of rain moves through the Treasure Coast. The National Weather Service forecast calls for a 95% chance of precipitation Thursday, with about 1.74 inches of rain possible. The district said saturated conditions were a key factor in its decision to cancel classes and close offices. “With ground conditions already saturated, we cannot be confident that students and staff will be able to travel safely to and from school,” the district said. “Weather conditions may also affect staff members’ ability to report to work.” The closure comes about two weeks after prolonged rainfall caused significant flooding in Indian River County. A flood watch for Indian River County remains in effect through Friday evening. The National Weather Service is also reporting a high surf advisory and rip current statement for the area. Indian River County officials have warned residents that roads not officially listed as closed could still have standing water or other hazards. Drivers should obey barricades and never attempt to drive through floodwater. The school district said student, family and employee safety remains its highest priority. Officials will continue monitoring conditions and said any additional information will be released through official district communication channels. A historic Vero Beach neighborhood is getting a new life through art, as sculptor Ross Power leads an effort to transform Edgewood into a vibrant community of artists, galleries, studios and public gathering spaces.Known as the "Father of the Vero Beach Art Village," Power is helping turn a once-overlooked neighborhood into a destination for creativity, where artists can live, work and share their talents.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The transformation is already underway, with murals, public art and community projects taking shape. Power says more galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are in the works, bringing new opportunities for artists, residents and visitors.A historic Vero Beach neighborhood becomes a canvasUnder the shade of a century-old lychee tree, Power reads from a poem dedicated to the tree as a dancer performs beneath its branches."A place where you and me can become we," Power said.For the longtime sculptor, the tree represents something bigger: a gathering place where art can bring people together.That vision is unfolding in Edgewood, a neighborhood established in 1916 that was once home to Vero Beach's first public school and first motel, according to the Vero Beach Art Village organization.Over the years, parts of the neighborhood fell into disrepair. But where others saw aging properties and neglected alleyways, Power saw potential."It spoke to me, and I heard I was once great and now I have fallen into disrepair and not respected at all, and I said we're going to change that," Power told WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts during a tour of the neighborhood.Power has spent decades creating art and helping develop artistic communities, including an art center in Miami.Now, he's bringing that experience to Vero Beach, with an entire neighborhood as his canvas.Turning Edgewood's alleyways into works of artOne of Power's biggest ambitions is transforming 11 alleyways throughout Edgewood into colorful destinations filled with murals and public art."I'm taking the alleys which are the ugliest part of the neighborhood and turning them into mural opportunities where the alleys are going to be like unbelievable for people to come and visit," Power said."There's a lack of buildings but there's not a lack of fences."Power sees those fences, walls and underused spaces as opportunities to showcase local artists and create an outdoor art experience.But the effort goes beyond beautifying back streets.Special zoning allows artists to live and work in the villageThe city of Vero Beach has established Cultural Arts Village zoning districts designed to encourage artistic businesses while preserving Edgewood's historic residential character.According to the city and the Vero Beach Art Village organization, the zoning creates opportunities for art galleries, studios, live-work spaces and other businesses, depending on the property's classification and applicable approvals.The goal is to create a walkable neighborhood where historic homes can become studios and galleries, and artists can collaborate with their neighbors.“I’ve been working on a bunch of different paintings. And we have projects; there's a bunch of different projects we’ve been working on whether it’s for the city or for trying to save big blue, or our community garden, “ said Linwood Addison Fuller IV, an artist who moved to Edgewood for the focus on art. His wife is also an artist.“It’s so much better to be an artist in a community with other artists,” said sculptor Andrew Draminski. “I’m sitting here working and my neighbors are walking their dog down the alley and come on in and we have a cup of coffee or something like that.”The village's vision extends beyond traditional galleries. Organizers hope to create spaces for music, dance, poetry, photography, workshops and other community events.More galleries, studios and community spaces plannedAccording to the nonprofit Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village, the neighborhood's transformation is a grassroots effort involving artists, residents, businesses and volunteers.The organization highlights ongoing initiatives involving murals, public art, studios, galleries, streetscape improvements and community events.Power says additional galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are also in the works.For him, the goal isn't simply to attract visitors. It's to create a community where artists can thrive together and residents can take pride in their neighborhood."If you want to eat great food, hear great music, see great things, meet great artists, this is the place," Power said.And beneath the sprawling branches of that century-old lychee tree, Power hopes the community he's helping cultivate will continue to grow.Where is the Vero Beach Art Village?The Vero Beach Art Village is located in the historic Edgewood neighborhood, just west of downtown Vero Beach.The neighborhood generally stretches between 14th and 20th avenues and 18th and 20th streets.The Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village nonprofit encourages residents and visitors to support the effort through volunteering, donations and participation in community art projects.Click here for more information about the village, its projects and opportunities to get involved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. If you've ever admired a perfectly golden Thanksgiving turkey and wondered how professional chefs make it look so good, Okeechobee Steakhouse co-owner Ralph Lewis has a surprisingly simple answer."It's butter."And not just a little butter.During a recent Thanksgiving cooking demonstration at Okeechobee Prime Meat Market, Lewis stood beside a giant inflatable stick of butter, worked from a table piled high with butter and seasonings, and even pulled a backup rubber stick of butter from his pocket.For Lewis, butter isn't simply an ingredient. It's the foundation of a great Thanksgiving turkey."Are you really supposed to have a budget with butter?" Lewis joked. "Those two words do not go together."According to Lewis, the biggest mistake many home cooks make is putting all of their butter on the outside of the bird.Instead, he recommends carefully separating the skin from the breast meat and creating pockets beneath the skin.Once those pockets are created, it's time to start adding butter.Lots of butter."You just want to keep working it in there," Lewis said. That's impossible, literally impossible, and that's a chef's code."As the turkey cooks, the butter melts beneath the skin, helping keep the meat moist while contributing to the rich color and flavor many Thanksgiving hosts are trying to achieve.After working butter beneath the skin, Lewis also coats the outside of the turkey before adding seasoning.One of the most useful tips Lewis shared involves seasoning the butter before it ever touches the bird.Start by taking butter out of the refrigerator and allowing it to soften to room temperature.Then combine the softened butter with herbs and seasonings such as:Kosher saltFreshly ground black pepperThymeRosemarySageMix everything together until it forms a seasoned compound butter.Then spread that butter beneath the skin and across the exterior of the turkey.By combining the herbs and seasoning directly into the butter, the flavors are distributed more evenly throughout the turkey as it cooks.Lewis says it's a simple step that can make a noticeable difference in flavor.Allow butter to come to room temperature.Mix the butter with kosher salt, black pepper, thyme, rosemary, sage or your favorite herbs.Gently separate the skin from the breast meat without tearing it.Spread seasoned butter beneath the skin and continue working it throughout the breast area.Coat the exterior of the turkey with additional butter.Add additional herbs and seasoning as desired.Place about a half-inch to one inch of water, chicken stock or turkey stock in the bottom of the pan.Cover the turkey with foil and roast at approximately 325 degrees.About 30 minutes before the turkey is done, remove the foil and increase the heat.Lewis says this final step helps create the deep golden-brown color that makes a Thanksgiving turkey look picture-perfect.Of course, Lewis' demonstration included a healthy helping of humor.At one point, while explaining his butter-heavy technique, he declared there is no such thing as too much butter.When told that Thanksgiving calories don't count, he quickly fired back:"What's calories?"And when asked whether anything should go inside the turkey cavity itself, his answer was immediate."Well, butter, of course."For families looking to spend less time in the kitchen and more time around the dinner table, Okeechobee Prime Meat Market is offering a variety of Thanksgiving meal packages featuring roasted or smoked turkeys, prime rib, beef tenderloin, traditional sides and holiday desserts.The market's Ultimate Holiday Family Feast serves 16 to 18 people and includes a Bell & Evans all-natural turkey, prime roasted beef tenderloin, stuffing, mashed potatoes, gravy, cranberry sauce and more.Pre-orders are available through Okeechobee Prime Meat Market in West Palm Beach.This article was drafted with the assistance of Microsoft Copilot using reporting, interview transcripts, and information gathered by WPTV journalist T.A. All facts, quotes, and editorial decisions were reviewed by WPTV before publication.What do you want me to Shine A Light on? What are you most proud of where you live? Email me at tawalker@wptv.com.

Lucie homeowner says recent heavy rain is worsening damage left behind by Hurricane Milton more than two years ago, as she continues waiting for repairs through the state's Rebuild Florida Housing Repair and Replacement Program. A repair assessment reviewed by WPTV documents unrepaired storm damage and work needed inside her home.WATCH: Recent rainfall worsens Hurricane Milton damage at Port St. Lucie homeCaryn McGregor contacted WPTV asking for help as water continued entering her house through the ceiling, windows and vents. During WPTV's visit, rainwater could be seen dripping inside the home."I'm scared my ceiling's gonna come down," McGregor said.Buckets and towels have become a temporary solution while she waits for more permanent repairs."Water is coming in our house, and we're experiencing so much now," McGregor said. "I just can't believe the events that are happening."Assessment documents unrepaired Hurricane Milton damageMcGregor said her roof was damaged when Hurricane Milton struck Florida in October 2024. She said she initially contacted her insurance company but couldn't afford the deductible and later sought help through Rebuild Florida.A repair assessment reviewed by WPTV lists Oct. 9, 2024, as the date of loss and says McGregor's home was inspected Jan. 6, 2026.The assessment documents unrepaired storm damage and says McGregor reported plumbing problems since the hurricane. The proposed scope of work includes repairs involving ceilings, walls, plumbing, siding, appliances, drywall and doors.The document helps establish the damage identified during the Rebuild Florida assessment, but it does not establish whether the proposed repairs were ultimately approved or funded.Recent rain adds to homeowner's concernsMcGregor told WPTV the continued water intrusion has left her worried that parts of the ceiling could collapse."I can't even have my son living here because the ceiling, I'm scared of it falling on him and hurting him," McGregor said. She also expressed concerns about water and mold.McGregor said water has damaged appliances in the home, including her washer, dryer and dishwasher."The water is ruining everything," she said.Homeowner says she's waiting on permits and repairsMcGregor said Rebuild Florida inspected the home in January but the repairs have not been completed."They were supposed to help," she said. "However they were going to rebuild or replace it, they were supposed to do that."McGregor said she has been told the project is waiting on permits before work can move forward. The documents reviewed by WPTV do not establish which permits remain outstanding, when they were requested or when construction is expected to begin.For McGregor, recent rainfall has added urgency to a problem she says has already kept her family from returning to normal."I want them to help us fix our house," she said. "They said they were going to."WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache reached out to Rebuild Florida seeking answers about the delay, the permitting process and when work could begin. Rebuild Florida acknowledged receiving WPTV's request, but a response addressing those questions had not been received by the time of reporting.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

The historic flooding that hit St. Lucie County in early November left hundreds of homes damaged and raised questions about whether the region’s drainage system can handle another major storm. Those concerns are growing as more heavy rain moves through the area this week. The CBS12 News I-Team looked at who oversees the system and what officials say needs to improve. South Florida’s drainage system is a network of canals, ponds, and locks overseen by multiple agencies. Lucie County, responsibilities are shared by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the South Florida Water Management District, the county, cities, local water-control districts, and homeowners’ associations. Who is responsible can depend on the specific canal or drainage system. Lucie County Commissioner Cathy Townsend, who has criticized the water management district, said, It was beyond anything any of us could have imagined. More than three days of rain brought over a foot of water to parts of the county, with some areas receiving as much as 17 inches. As water rose, residents called Townsend asking what was being done. They were asking what’s being done. And unfortunately, there wasn’t anything I could tell them except the floodgates are open and the water is flowing, she said. Rain normally drains into ditches and canals and moves toward the St. Lucie River and Indian River Lagoon before flowing out to the ocean. But the heavy rainfall coincided with unusually high tides, limiting the system’s ability to move water out. This was the perfect storm, Townsend said. The king tide, high tide, 20 inches of rain everything was against us. At a water management district meeting days later, board members discussed the condition of the region’s infrastructure. Board member Thomas Hurley called the flooding a wake-up call and said maintaining the system is increasingly important as water levels rise. Board member Jay Steinle said deficiencies in forecasting equipment left the district without enough warning to draw down canals and prepare. I’m surprised that things went as well as they did given we didn’t have any preparation, Steinle said. Lucie County prepares for more rain after historic flooding; schools closed Wednesday Nyla Pipes, a St. Lucie County resident and water-policy advocate, told the board that warnings had been raised before the flooding. I happened to know that those alarm bells had sounded some weeks before, but many for the past several years, she said. The flooding also exposed vulnerabilities in newer, master-planned communities such as Tradition. In the Vitalia neighborhood, floodwaters covered streets, stranded vehicles, and left some residents without power for days. One possible factor is how the community was built: Tradition relied on the existing canal system, and developers were not required to build a new canal, according to the reporting in the CBS12 News I-Team’s investigation. Townsend said the county needs to do more to maintain its canals and ditches. She also believes the water management district took too long to open one of the canals. She later learned the delay was related to an environmental concern. In my opinion, I do think that the 23 canals could have been opened a lot earlier, she said. Townsend said it is unclear whether opening the canals sooner would have prevented the flooding, given the amount of water the system could take. CBS12 News reached out to the South Florida Water Management District for comment and will update this story when it responds. The flooding also raised insurance concerns. Many of the flooded areas were outside FEMA’s high-risk flood zones, where flood insurance is generally required for federally backed mortgages. Some homeowners in those areas may not have had flood insurance to help cover the damage.

The advisory affects customers in Tradition, Riverland, Western Grove, Wilson Grove, Southern Grove, Copper Creek, Wylder and Verano, as well as properties along Glades Cut Off Road. For Marcus Rowe, the first sign of trouble was a sudden drop in water pressure. "I went to turn on the faucet, and the water pressure was low. I was like, 'what's going on'?" See also: 'We can all do something': Couple urges action for children in foster care City officials said water quality sampling is underway, but the boil water notice will remain in effect until laboratory testing confirms the water is safe to drink. Because of the large number of customers affected, officials said the advisory could remain in place beyond the initial 48-hour timeframe. For the Rowe family, that has meant relying on bottled water and boiling water for daily needs. "Boiling water, doing what they told us to do," Rowe said. "It's something small, I'm not really sweating it. We're going as far as turning on the water in the fridge so the ice doesn't get accumulated with that tainted water." Residents are advised to continue boiling water used for drinking, cooking, making ice, brushing teeth and washing dishes until the city announces the notice has been lifted. A 24-year-old woman riding her e-scooter to work was critically injured in a hit-and-run early Monday morning near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace in Port St. Body camera footage shows police responding to the scene, where the woman was found unconscious in the road. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said the driver left the scene without stopping to render aid or contact law enforcement. Detectives identified the vehicle and traced it back to 18-year-old Tristan Sanchez Chasmer. According to Niemczyk, Chasmer and two passengers had just ding-dong ditched a home about a mile from the crash site. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 "He was trying to get away from playing a prank," Niemczyk said. "So I think it would be reasonable to conclude that he was not driving with all due care that he normally would." Niemczyk said the two passengers exited the truck shortly after the crash, but none of them called 911. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. "They're aware that they hit something. I'll say that," Niemczyk said. A witness called 911 and helped the victim, who was airlifted to the hospital. She remains in critical condition. "We're deeply concerned for her recovery and our thoughts are with her loved ones," Niemczyk said. Chasmer was arrested on one count of fleeing the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury and is being held on a $5,000 bond. The two passengers are not facing charges.

Lucie County residents are preparing for heavy rainfall this week, with officials offering free self-serve sandbag stations and working to clear drainage systems to address potential flooding. Another resident shared their concerns, saying, "My crawlspace got a foot of water in there, so trying to get all these bags to try and cover up the opening, you know." Public works crews in St. Lucie County are actively checking and clearing swales and drainage systems as the area braces for more severe weather. Recent flooding left parts of the county submerged, with residents in the Creekside development trapped inside, some using kayaks to navigate flooded streets while others waded through the water. Fredrick Reeves, a resident whose home was previously flooded, is preparing for the upcoming rain by using sandbags and mulch to block water from entering his house. "It was pretty bad, and the house itself, once it started coming in, I thought maybe we would be alright. I threw down all my clothes trying to soak it up, but that didn't do anything. The next thing you knew, it was in the house," Reeves said. He described the situation as "overwhelming." Just two weeks after historic flooding forced schools to close for three straight days, St. Lucie County students are getting another day off as more heavy rain threatens the area. Lucie Public Schools announced Tuesday that all schools and district offices will be closed Wednesday due to the threat of significant rainfall and localized flooding. The announcement comes after the district dismissed students two hours early Tuesday as worsening weather conditions raised concerns about flooding. It's the latest disruption for the district, which was forced to close schools for three consecutive days Nov. 4, 5 and 6 after historic flooding left roads underwater and communities struggling to recover. Lucie County clears drains, prepares for more rain after historic flooding Now, with the ground already saturated, district leaders say they aren't taking any chances. According to the district, forecasts from the National Weather Service indicate the potential for significant rainfall, although uncertainty remains about exactly when and where the heaviest rain will fall. "Given the already saturated conditions in our community, the District believes taking a cautious approach is in the best interest of our students, families, and employees," district officials said in a statement. John Carroll High School also announced it will be closed Wednesday, Nov. 18, due to the threat of heavy rainfall and flooding across the region. The decision follows an early dismissal Tuesday and a review of weather forecasts and local flooding conditions. School officials said all Wednesday activities, including athletics, practices, extracurricular programs and other events, have been canceled. John Carroll anticipates reopening Thursday, pending weather and road conditions. Administrators will continue monitoring forecasts and coordinating with local authorities before making further decisions. Updates will be shared through the school's official communication channels. All after-school activities, aftercare programs, and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday have also been canceled. District officials said they will continue monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures, and access to schools, bus stops, and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision on whether schools will reopen Thursday is expected Wednesday evening. Families are encouraged to monitor the district's official website and social media channels for updates.

Indian River County officials are preparing for the possibility of more flooding as heavy rain threatens areas already impacted by recent storms. Emergency management officials said the ground is saturated, and additional heavy rain could lead to flooding in areas that did not flood during the last storm. Earlier this month, the county dealt with flooded neighborhoods, impassable roads, and traffic disruptions. Officials are closely monitoring flood-prone communities, including Heritage Plantation, Whispering Palms, and areas near Highland Drive, as they remain concerned about incoming weather conditions. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Ryan Lloyd, who serves as the Deputy Director and Emergency Management Chief for the Indian River County Department of Emergency Services, is concerned about the weather that could be heading this way. "There could be areas that flood that we're not expecting per se or that necessarily flooded in the past," Lloyd said. So, we're asking that our residents be prepared countywide for any type of flood event that could occur over the next 72 hours." Lloyd has a message for the public. "We also ask our residents to please not do flood tours where they're going out just by standing and looking on at flooded neighborhoods, as they drive through those neighborhoods," Lloyd said. "It can create waves that actually go into the houses, and it can make the flooding even worse for residents." Visitors Ed and Jackie Brookes shared their thoughts on the situation. "That's unusual for Florida. I'm here to get more and more of the extreme weather here, but we're just glad to be with our family. It's still beautiful, visitor Ed Brookes said. hero.headline: Indian River County public schools to close Friday as flooding shuts roads
hero.body:
Public schools across Indian River County will be closed Friday, Nov. 20, after flooding left more roads impassable and raised concerns about additional rain. The School District of Indian River County announced the decision Thursday, pointing to localized flooding, already saturated ground and the potential for more heavy rainfall. District officials said the shutdown was intended to protect students, their families and school employees. The announcement applies to all of the county’s public schools. It comes as road closures increase, particularly in Vero Lake Estates, and water levels rise at the district’s North County Transportation compound.

The county’s road closure map showed nine road closures and four lane closures Thursday. Among the roads listed as closed were 100th Court, 103rd Avenue, 104th Avenue, 83rd Street and 87th Street. Those five roads were part of the larger set of closures shown on the map, rather than a complete list of affected roads. Vero Lake Estates was a particular concern in both the district’s closure announcement and the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office’s flooding reports. The district cited the growing number of road closures there, while the sheriff’s office reported additional flooded roads in the neighborhood.

Deputies warned motorists against driving into standing water. Floodwater can be deeper than it looks, and vehicles can stall after entering it, according to the sheriff’s office. That warning accompanied the agency’s reports of more flooded roads in Vero Lake Estates. High-water vehicles are in the area, and anyone who becomes stranded should call 911. The safety message applies even when a driver cannot judge the depth of water covering a road: its appearance may not reflect how deep it actually is. The sheriff’s office’s advice was to stay out of the water rather than attempt to drive through it.

A flood watch remains in effect for Indian River County through Friday evening, with additional showers and thunderstorms possible. The National Weather Service reported that parts of eastern Indian River County had received 2 to 4 inches of rain. The possibility of further rainfall, combined with saturated ground and existing flooding, was among the reasons the district gave for canceling Friday’s classes. Beyond the weather-related closure, schools will also be closed for Thanksgiving break. The district’s immediate concern Thursday was the flooding affecting local roads and its North County Transportation compound, with Friday’s shutdown intended to keep students, families and employees safe.

cards.headline: Flooded roads disrupt Indian River County travel; trash service could be affected
cards.teaser: Officials urged drivers to avoid flooded roads in Vero Lake Estates and watch two potential trouble spots in Fellsmere. Unsafe conditions could also disrupt trash collection and close waste facilities early.
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office reported more flooded roads in Vero Lake Estates on Thursday as heavy rain moved through the county, while county officials warned that unsafe conditions could disrupt trash collection and waste facilities. The sheriff’s office urged drivers to stay off flooded roads because water can be deeper than it appears and can stall vehicles. High-water vehicles are in the area, and anyone who becomes stranded should call 911.

The county’s road closure map listed nine road closures and four lane closures as of 10:53 a.m. Thursday. Roads marked closed included 100th Court, 103rd Avenue, 104th Avenue, 83rd Street and 87th Street. Lane-closure listings included 101st Avenue and West 98th Avenue. In Fellsmere, the city urged drivers to use extreme caution and identified New York Avenue near Hickory Street and North Broadway as potential trouble spots. Those roads could close if rain continues, the city said. City Hall remains open and operating normally.

The county warned that heavy rain and gusty winds could disrupt trash collection. Residents whose streets are flooded were asked not to put their carts in the water. The landfill and customer convenience centers could close early if conditions become unsafe.

A flood watch remains in effect for Indian River County through Friday evening, with more showers and thunderstorms possible. The National Weather Service issued a flood advisory Thursday morning for eastern Indian River and northeastern St. Lucie counties after 2 to 4 inches of rain fell in parts of the area. The advisory warned of minor flooding in low-lying and poorly drained areas. The School District of Indian River County closed all public schools and district offices Thursday, saying saturated ground and expected rain could make travel unsafe for students and staff.

cards.headline: Indian River County extends flood emergency through Nov. 23 after storm damage
cards.teaser: The county reported two properties destroyed and seven with major damage as of Tuesday. Officials warn that more heavy rain could flood areas that escaped the previous storm.
cards.body:
Indian River County has extended its local state of emergency through Monday, Nov. 23, as officials prepare for more rain and the possibility of additional flooding in areas already affected by recent storms. As of Tuesday, the county reported that the previous storm had destroyed two properties and caused major damage to seven others. Another 65 properties had minor damage, and 97 others were affected. Earlier this month, flooding inundated neighborhoods, left roads impassable and disrupted traffic across the county.

Emergency management officials said the ground is saturated, creating a risk that additional heavy rain could cause flooding in places that did not flood during the last storm. Officials are closely monitoring flood-prone communities, including Heritage Plantation, Whispering Palms and areas near Highland Drive. Ryan Lloyd, deputy director and emergency management chief for the Indian River County Department of Emergency Services, urged residents throughout the county to prepare for a possible flood event over the next 72 hours. “There could be areas that flood that we're not expecting per se or that necessarily flooded in the past,” Lloyd said.

Lloyd also asked residents not to drive through flooded neighborhoods simply to look at the damage, warning that their vehicles could worsen conditions for people whose homes were already threatened by water. “It can create waves that actually go into the houses, and it can make the flooding even worse for residents,” he said. His request came as county officials remained concerned about incoming weather and the potential for more flooding beyond the locations affected by the previous storm.

Crews spent the day cleaning swales and inspecting drainage systems across Indian River County as officials prepared for the possibility of more rain. The county’s emergency information center is open to answer questions about the flood threat. Residents can call 772-226-4000 for assistance.

hero.headline: Boil water notice extended 24 hours for 21,000 customers in western Port St. Lucie
hero.body:
A precautionary boil water notice for about 21,000 customers in western Port St. Lucie has been extended by 24 hours as the city continues water-quality testing after a contractor struck a major water main. The contractor was working on a non-city construction project when the 36-inch main was hit near Glades Cut Off Road. Crews finished repairs Tuesday evening and began flushing the water system. Water service has been fully restored, but the precautionary notice remains in place. Customers must continue boiling water for drinking and other specified uses until the city announces that the notice has been lifted.

The affected area includes Tradition, Riverland, Western Grove, Wilson Grove, Southern Grove, Copper Creek, Wylder and Verano. Properties along Glades Cut Off Road are also covered by the advisory. City officials said water-quality sampling is underway and laboratory results must confirm that the water is safe to drink before the notice can end. Officials also said the number of customers affected means the advisory could continue beyond its initial 48-hour timeframe. The 24-hour extension gives the city more time to complete testing, with the notice still dependent on confirmation that the water is safe.

For resident Marcus Rowe, a sudden loss of water pressure was the first indication that something was wrong. “I went to turn on the faucet, and the water pressure was low. I was like, 'what's going on'?” he said. Since the disruption, his family has relied on bottled water and boiled water to meet daily needs. Rowe said the family was following the instructions while taking the inconvenience in stride. “Boiling water, doing what they told us to do,” he said. “It's something small, I'm not really sweating it.” His family is continuing those precautions while the advisory remains active.

Residents covered by the notice are advised to boil water used for drinking, cooking, making ice, brushing their teeth and washing dishes. Those instructions remain in effect despite the restoration of water service and the completion of repairs to the broken main. For households such as the Rowes, that means continuing to use bottled water or boil water for daily needs rather than returning to normal use of tap water. The city has said the notice will stay in place until laboratory testing confirms the water is safe to drink. Customers should continue the precautions until the city announces that the advisory has ended.

cards.headline: Driver arrested in Port St. Lucie hit-and-run that critically injured e-scooter rider
cards.teaser: Tristan Sanchez Chasmer, 18, is being held on a $5,000 bond. Police say he and two passengers had just played a prank at a home about a mile from the crash site.
cards.body:
An 18-year-old driver was arrested in a Port St. Lucie hit-and-run that critically injured a 24-year-old woman riding an e-scooter to work early Monday. Tristan Sanchez Chasmer faces one count of fleeing the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury and is being held on a $5,000 bond.

The crash happened near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Body camera footage shows officers responding to the scene, where the woman was found unconscious in the road. A witness called 911 and helped her before she was airlifted to the hospital. She remains in critical condition.

Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said the driver left without stopping to render aid or contact law enforcement. Detectives identified the vehicle and traced it to Chasmer. According to Niemczyk, Chasmer and two passengers had just ding-dong ditched a home about a mile from the crash site. “He was trying to get away from playing a prank,” Niemczyk said.

Niemczyk said the two passengers exited the truck shortly after the crash, but none of the three called 911. “They're aware that they hit something. I'll say that,” he said. The two passengers are not facing charges.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie police use GTA VI launch to warn against reckless driving
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie Police Department used Thursday’s Grand Theft Auto VI launch to remind fans that reckless driving and other crimes carry consequences beyond a video game. In a lighthearted safety message, police warned that U.S. 1 and Crosstown are not places to race and that drivers cannot restart after a real-world crash. The department borrowed the game’s wanted-level system to urge residents to avoid attracting police attention. Its reminders included obeying red lights, keeping vehicles off sidewalks and leaving patrol cars alone. Police also joked about avoiding an encounter with the SWAT team, encouraging players to keep the game’s lawbreaking on screen.

Grand Theft Auto VI officially launches Nov. 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. Its fictional state, Leonida, is modeled on Florida, with the Miami-inspired Vice City at its center. The story follows Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos as their criminal plans draw them into a statewide conspiracy. Florida has also become part of the game’s promotion. In September, a large pink sign welcoming visitors to Vice City appeared on Miami’s Kaseya Center under an agreement between Miami-Dade County and Rockstar Games. County officials expected the arrangement to generate nearly $1 million in revenue and provide marketing opportunities. The Miami Heat held a Vice City-themed celebration Wednesday, with a Thursday launch party planned at the Clevelander South Beach and a Rockstar festival scheduled for Saturday.

Other police agencies have used the release to distinguish fictional crimes from real offenses. Atlanta police warned against reckless driving, impaired driving, vehicle theft and violence. In South Florida, law enforcement leaders questioned public involvement in promoting the game. The Miami-Dade Association of Chiefs of Police opposed marketing the county as Vice City, citing depictions of violence against women and police officers. Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz also questioned whether public agencies should promote a game centered on crimes her department works to stop. Port St. Lucie’s message focused on safe driving and keeping virtual criminal behavior away from local roads.

The launch could also disrupt work and viewing habits. A GameSquare survey of 1,000 U.S. employees found that 10% of full-time respondents who identified as gamers planned to miss work on launch day, while another 30% were considering time off. Among those considering an absence, 36% said they would report being sick. Forty-two percent expected lower productivity. Surveyed gamers anticipated spending about $400 on the game and related purchases and playing a median of 15 hours during the opening weekend. Seventy percent said they might skip sports to play, and 42% expected to be less likely to watch NFL games that weekend. Indian River County students had Thursday off because of forecast weather and flooding concerns, while St. Lucie schools reopened.

Police are monitoring conditions and urge drivers to use alternate routes around flooded areas. Drivers should not drive through standing or moving water, go around barricades or enter closed roads.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie homeowner says rain is worsening unrepaired Hurricane Milton damage
cards.teaser: Caryn McGregor says water is entering through her ceiling, windows and vents as she awaits Rebuild Florida assistance. A repair assessment documents unrepaired storm damage and proposed work inside her home.
cards.body:
Recent heavy rain is worsening unrepaired Hurricane Milton damage at Caryn McGregor's Port St. Lucie home, she said. She is awaiting assistance through the state's Rebuild Florida Housing Repair and Replacement Program, which provides housing repairs or replacement.

Water continues to enter through the ceiling, windows and vents, with rainwater observed dripping inside the house. McGregor is using buckets and towels while she waits for permanent repairs. “I'm scared my ceiling's gonna come down,” she said.

A repair assessment lists Oct. 9, 2024, as the date of loss and Jan. 6, 2026, as the date her home was inspected. It documents unrepaired storm damage and says McGregor reported plumbing problems since the hurricane. The proposed work includes repairs involving ceilings, walls, plumbing, siding, appliances, drywall and doors.

McGregor said her roof was damaged when Hurricane Milton struck Florida in October 2024. She initially contacted her insurance company but could not afford the deductible, she said. She later sought help through Rebuild Florida and said the repairs remain unfinished after the January inspection.

McGregor said she has been told the project is waiting on permits before work can proceed. The assessment documents the damage identified during the inspection and the proposed repairs.

The continued water intrusion has left McGregor worried about water, mold and the ceiling collapsing. “I can't even have my son living here because the ceiling, I'm scared of it falling on him and hurting him,” she said. She also said water has damaged her washer, dryer and dishwasher.

“I want them to help us fix our house,” McGregor said. “They said they were going to.”

hero.headline: Martin County sheriff readies high-water vehicles in Stuart and Indiantown
hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff’s Office is preparing high-water rescue vehicles in Stuart and Indiantown for expected heavy rain and potential flooding, with a team on standby for urgent calls from the emergency operations center.

Two high-water vehicles are at the sheriff’s office in Stuart, and another is stationed in Indiantown in case that area floods. The preparations are part of Martin County officials’ response to expected heavy rainfall across the Treasure Coast.

Sheriff John Budensiek describes the retired military vehicles, known as MTVs, as the agency’s worst-case-scenario vehicles for natural disasters such as hurricanes and flash flooding. They sit high off the ground and are heavy enough to drive through hurricane-force winds and high water.

“Hopefully we don't need them. But we're in a position where if we get the rains that are expected and if we get the flooding that we've had here in the last couple of weeks, again, we're prepared to try to help our citizens as best we can,” Budensiek said.
